results.title: High insurance costs push new car owners towards repairs outside dealerships
results.description: Dubai: Car dealership officials said higher insurance premiums for repairs carried out at dealerships are prompting some customers to have their vehicles repaired at external workshops instead. They said the trend has had little impact on the operating revenues of dealerships and their repair workshops because their businesses also depend on vehicle sales, periodic maintenance unrelated to insurance and the supply of spare parts. They said vehicle owners are more affected by the policies of some insurers, particularly higher premiums for policies covering dealership repairs. Motorists said high insurance premiums for newer cars that include dealership repairs are forcing them to choose cheaper policies covering repairs at external workshops, depriving them of the benefits of dealership servicing. They also said some insurers impose strict conditions for obtaining favourable prices for dealership repairs in the second year of vehicle ownership, including requirements relating to accident history, even in cases involving minor accidents or unknown parties. Motorists’ concerns Customer Youssef Abdul Majeed said: “The insurance companies I contacted imposed high prices on the insurance policy in case of repairs inside the agency, even though my car is new and I bought it last year.” He added: “I was forced to accept an insurance policy for repairs outside the agency, even though the policy price is lower than policies that include repairs inside the agency.” Customer Ali Ibrahim said: “Insurance companies are supposed to provide reasonable prices for repairs at dealerships, especially for new cars. It is unreasonable for a car to be new and for us to have to repair it in external workshops and (garages) in the second or third year after purchase.” He added: “Insurance companies impose difficult conditions for repairs within the agency, including not being involved in any accident in the first year of buying the car, even if the accident was minor or against an unknown party, for reasons beyond the control of the vehicle owner or his participation in the accident.” He said some insurance policies cost between Dh500 and Dh700 more when dealership repairs are included, compared with policies covering repairs at external garages. Customer Hamza Hussein said: “The high insurance premiums for repairing new vehicles at dealerships force us to use external repair shops, depriving us of the benefits of dealership repairs and maintaining the quality and safety of our cars during the second or third year after purchase.” He called for a review of insurance premiums and the conditions governing dealership repairs, particularly for newer vehicles. Dealership revenues Wissam Khalil, General Manager of Porsche Cars Center - Abu Dhabi, said: “The higher prices of insurance policies for repairs within dealerships have little impact on the operating revenues of car dealerships, which are linked to several other criteria, most notably periodic maintenance that is not related to insurance, and the provision of spare parts for maintenance operations.” He said vehicle owners are more affected by the policies adopted by some insurance companies for newer cars, particularly higher premiums for policies covering dealership repairs. Higher repair costs Khaled Al-Asal, sales manager for the GEC brand at Gargash Motors, said: “Some insurance companies resort to increasing insurance prices for repairs within dealerships, due to the higher cost at dealerships compared to external repair workshops.” Al-Asal said these insurance practices have little impact on dealership operating revenues because dealerships also focus on sales and periodic maintenance. He added: “Imposing high prices for an insurance policy that includes repairing a newly purchased car inside the dealership may affect the safety and quality of the car if unsuitable external repair workshops are chosen. This requires customers to choose external repair workshops of suitable quality to maintain their new vehicles in case they have to choose an insurance policy that does not allow repairs inside the dealership during the first three years of purchase.” Mohamed Salah, a sales consultant at a car dealership, said preventing owners of newer cars from benefiting from dealership repairs because of higher insurance premiums could affect vehicles if motorists choose lower-quality external workshops. He said dealerships offer trained technicians, appropriate original spare parts and the ability to fit components correctly. Insurers cite cost differences Adnan Elias, sales manager at Fidelity Insurance Services, said: “Insurance companies are forced to impose higher fees on insurance policies that include repairs within dealerships, even if the vehicles are new, due to the significantly higher cost of repairs at dealerships compared to external workshops, thus avoiding any potential losses for insurance companies in exchange for the high cost of repairs.” On benefits for motorists with no accident history, he said: “It is natural that a customer who does not experience accidents during the first year of purchasing the car receives price advantages for repairs at the dealership, compared to someone who experiences accidents, and therefore has a higher chance of experiencing accidents than others.” Mohammed Ibrahim, a sales consultant at an insurance services company, said higher premiums for policies covering dealership repairs for newer cars are common because of the higher cost of dealership repairs charged to insurers following accidents. He added: “It is difficult to review insurance policy prices in light of the continued high cost of repairs at agencies, compared to external workshops, and the significant price differences.”

results.title: Smog Can Trigger Eye Irritation, Dryness and Inflammation
results.description: Every year, the festive glow turns into a grey blanket over Delhi. Firecracker residue, stubble smoke, exhaust fumes and cold and still air all push pollution levels way beyond safe limits. Most discussions centre on the lungs, but the eyes suffer as much and often first. Why are eyes so vulnerable? Unlike skin, the surface of the eye is exposed and unprotected by any outer layer. It is also wet. The cornea is separated from the air by a thin film of tears. The tissue is irritated and its balance disturbed as fine particles such as PM2.5, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ozone dissolve into this film. The result is inflammation that can develop within hours of exposure to it. Common Problems The most common complaints are redness, itching, watering and a gritty burning sensation, usually due to allergic or irritant conjunctivitis. Dry eye is another big problem. Pollutants cause tears to evaporate quicker, leaving eyes tired and sore, especially for those who spend long hours on screens. Tiny particles can also scratch the cornea, causing pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision. Rubbing irritated eyes with unwashed hands can lead to the insertion of bacteria or viruses. Contact lens wearers are at extra risk, as particles can get trapped under the lens and grind against the cornea. People with existing allergies, glaucoma or chronic dry eye often find that their symptoms worsen during smog episodes. Children and older adults, with their weaker defences, need special attention How to Protect Your Eyes Simple habits make a real difference during heavy smog: ● Don't rub your eyes. Instead, when you come inside, wash your face and eyes with clean, cool water. ● Wraparound sunglasses or protective glasses for outside wear. On bad days, use spectacles instead of contact lenses. ● Only use preservative-free lubricating drops with your doctor’s approval. Do not use steroid or redness-relief drops without advice. ● “Keep windows closed during peak pollution hours and use an air purifier indoors if you can. ● Follow the 20-20-20 rule for screens: every twenty minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. ● Stay hydrated and blink frequently to spread the tear film evenly. ● Follow the 20-20-20 rule on screens: every twenty minutes, look twenty feet away for twenty seconds. ● Stay hydrated and blink often, which helps spread the tear film evenly. When to See a Doctor Mild irritation usually resolves with rest and clean water, but some signs should never be ignored. If you have severe pain, a sudden drop in vision, marked sensitivity to light, thick or sticky discharge, or redness that doesn't get better in a day or two, get prompt care from an eye specialist. Don’t wait. What starts as a simple infection or corneal injury can become serious.
